extract:
The Shins emerged from Albuquerque, New Mexico in the mid-1990s, growing out of the same local indie scene that birthed singer-songwriter James Mercer's previous band, Flake Music. Mercer originally formed The Shins as a side project around 1996 while Flake Music was still active, but by the end of the decade it had become his primary creative outlet. The early lineup included Mercer alongside Flake bandmates Jesse Sandoval on drums, Marty Crandall on keyboards, and Neal Langford on bass, with the group steeping itself in the literate jangle of bands like The Zombies, The Kinks, and Echo and the Bunnymen, as well as the lo-fi indie of contemporaries on labels like Sub Pop.

Their debut album, Oh, Inverted World, arrived on Sub Pop in 2001 and quickly became a landmark of early-2000s indie rock. Tracks like New Slang, Caring Is Creepy, and The Past and Pending paired Mercer's high, melancholic tenor with hazy production and chiming melodies, drawing comparisons to Brian Wilson-era Beach Boys filtered through a bedroom-pop sensibility. The follow-up, Chutes Too Narrow in 2003, sharpened the band's songwriting considerably, trading some of the debut's reverb-soaked atmosphere for cleaner arrangements and country-tinged moments on songs like Saint Simon, Kissing the Lipless, and Gone for Good.

The Shins' cultural breakthrough came largely through Zach Braff's 2004 film Garden State, whose soundtrack prominently featured New Slang and Caring Is Creepy, with Natalie Portman's character famously declaring that New Slang would change your life. The exposure helped propel their third album, Wincing the Night Away, to a number two debut on the Billboard 200 in 2007, an extraordinary chart position for a Sub Pop release at the time. That record, featuring singles Phantom Limb and Australia, expanded the band's palette with shoegaze textures and more elaborate production while retaining Mercer's knack for oblique, bittersweet lyricism.

After Wincing the Night Away, Mercer overhauled the lineup, parting ways with the original members and reconfiguring The Shins essentially as a vehicle for his songwriting backed by rotating collaborators. In the interim, he formed Broken Bells with producer Brian Burton, better known as Danger Mouse, releasing a self-titled debut in 2010. The Shins returned in 2012 with Port of Morrow on Mercer's own Aural Apothecary label in partnership with Columbia, featuring the single Simple Song, and followed it in 2017 with Heartworms, which Mercer largely self-produced.

Within the broader landscape of 2000s indie rock, The Shins stood alongside acts like Modest Mouse, Death Cab for Cutie, and Iron and Wine as standard-bearers for a literate, melody-driven strain of the genre, and they remain among the most commercially successful artists in Sub Pop's catalog. Critical reception has generally been warm if occasionally more reserved for the post-reshuffle albums, with Oh, Inverted World and Chutes Too Narrow widely regarded as their defining statements; Sub Pop issued a twentieth-anniversary remaster of the debut in 2021. Mercer has continued to tour under the Shins banner and to release music with Broken Bells, cementing a legacy as one of the more distinctive American songwriters of his generation.
title: The Shins
